newsitem.title: USA: Senate balanced budget amendment close to passing.
newsitem.headline: Senate balanced budget amendment close to passing.

text.p: Senate Republicans moved within striking distance of winning their top political goal, a balanced budget amendment to the U.S. Constitution, with the pledge on Tuesday of a key Democrat to back it.
Louisiana freshman Sen. Mary Landrieu said she will keep her campaign pledge and vote for the Republican-authored version, despite reservations.

Eyes then shifted to the lone undecided vote of freshman Democrat Robert Torricelli of New Jersey, who could decide the outcome of the amendment. He refused to comment, saying he would announce his decision on Wednesday. Torricelli voted for a similar amendment in the House of Representatives in 1995.

The amendment has the support of all 55 Republicans and nine Democrats with two more, Joe Biden of Delaware and Max Baucus of Montana, expected to vote for it as they did last year. It needs 67 votes to reach the two-thirds requirement.

Speaking to reporters, Landrieu said she preferred two less restrictive Democratic alternatives but would vote for the Republican version to keep a campaign pledge to vote for a balanced budget amendment.

"Based on many statements made during the campaign on this issue, I will cast a 'yes' vote, but with reservations," she said at a news conference. Landrieu was elected by a very narrow margin and the Senate Rules Committee is looking into allegations of fraud raised by her opponent Woody Jenkins.

A fiscal conservative and former state treasurer, Landrieu said she would not have voted for the Republican version if not for her campaign pledge. "I know a lot more about the subject now than I did during the campaign," she said.

President Bill Clinton opposes the balanced budget amendment but Landrieu's decision was not criticised by the White House. "I think she made a principled decision based on what she felt was in the best interests of her constituents ... It's obviously going to be a very close vote and we will continue to work hard to express our point of view," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said.

Sen. Tom Daschle, the leader of minority Democrats who had spoken optimistically of defeating the amendment, now raised concerns. "My momentum has lost a couple of wheels," he told reporters after Landrieu's news conference.
One vote would swing the outcome either way.

With Torricelli's decision still unannounced, Republican Leader Trent Lott of Mississippi did not declare victory. "The vote is not over until it is actually taken. I think there may still be some other senators who are wrestling with this though they have not said so publicly."

Lott called for a vote by next Tuesday although the Senate still must wade through numerous amendments, including three major Democratic proposals which sponsors promoted as ways to protect Social Security and give Congress leeway to help the economy during a recession.

The balanced budget amendment has been bogged down in the House over the Social Security issue and Republican leaders were looking to passage in the Senate to give it a boost. House Republicans postponed a Feb. 26 floor vote until they see the Senate outcome.

The amendment would require Washington to balance its books annually starting in 2002 or within two years of its enactment. However, it does not specify how Congress is to balance the budget and would permit deficits and borrowing if approved by three-fifths of Congress.
Within seven years of clearing Congress it must be ratified by 38 of 50 states to become part of the U.S. Constitution.

Meanwhile, White House budget director Franklin Raines warned that the balanced budget amendment crafted by Republicans could result in cuts in benefits if the government runs up against its budget ceiling late in a fiscal year.
If tax revenues were projected to drop below the expected spending during the year, spending would have to be adjusted to keep the budget balanced, he said in a letter to Daschle.
"Consequently, programmes with monthly payments would be unable to avoid exposure to such reductions," Raines wrote.
This view is challenged by Republicans who argue this would not be allowed to happen.
